notes.summary:
Internet, email and networking give 4 to 5 questions in the Tier 2 computer section. Past papers ask most about email, network devices and online threats, then protocols, IP addresses, the OSI model and browser shortcuts.

Most questions test a full form, what a device or protocol does, a port number or a size in bits. Learn the tables below line by line.

concepts.title: Internet and the World Wide Web
concepts.body:
• The Internet is a worldwide network of networks. It grew from ARPANET (1969), a project of the US Department of Defense.
  • The World Wide Web (WWW) is a service that runs on the Internet: linked web pages. It was invented by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989. He also wrote the first browser, called WorldWideWeb. Mosaic (1993) was the first popular graphical browser.
  • Internet and WWW are not the same: email and FTP use the Internet but are not part of the web.
  • A web page is one document written in HTML (HyperText Markup Language). A website is a group of related pages. The first page of a site is its home page.
  • A hyperlink is clickable text or a picture that opens another page. Hypertext is text with links in it.
  • An ISP (Internet Service Provider) such as BSNL, Jio or Airtel connects you to the Internet.
  • A search engine (Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo, Yahoo) finds pages. A browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari) opens and shows them.
  • An intranet is a private network inside one organisation; an extranet lets chosen outsiders such as suppliers into it.

concepts.title: URL and domain names
concepts.body:
A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the full address of a resource on the web.

Part of https://www.example.co.in/news/today.htmlName
httpsProtocol (scheme)
www.example.co.inDomain name (host). "in" is the top-level domain
/news/today.htmlPath to the page or file
Top-level domainUsed by
.comCommercial
.orgOrganisation, often non-profit
.netNetwork providers
.eduEducation (US)
.govGovernment (US); India uses .gov.in
.milUS military
.intInternational bodies
.in, .uk, .jpCountry codes (India, United Kingdom, Japan)

A URL cannot contain spaces. The part before :// is the protocol; the part after the first single / is the path.

concepts.title: Web browsers and cookies
concepts.body:
BrowserMade byRendering engine
Google ChromeGoogle (2008)Blink
Microsoft EdgeMicrosoft (2015), replaced Internet ExplorerBlink (since 2020)
Internet ExplorerMicrosoft (1995), retired in 2022Trident
Mozilla FirefoxMozilla (2004)Gecko
SafariApple (2003)WebKit
OperaOpera (1995)Blink
  • The rendering engine (layout engine) is the part of a browser that reads HTML and CSS and displays the web page.
  • Cache stores copies of pages and images so they load faster next time. History lists pages visited. A bookmark (favourite) saves a page address.
  • Incognito (private) mode does not save history or cookies after the window is closed. It does not hide you from your ISP or employer.
  • A cookie is a small text file a website stores in your browser to remember you (login, cart, settings). Session cookies are deleted when the browser closes; persistent cookies stay until they expire. First-party cookies come from the site you visit; third-party (tracking) cookies come from other sites, such as advertisers, and track you across sites, which exposes your privacy.
  • A plug-in or extension adds features to a browser.
Keys (Chrome, Edge, Firefox on Windows)What it does

concepts.title: IP addresses, MAC and DNS
concepts.body:
AddressSizeWritten asCount or note
IPv432 bits4 numbers 0 to 255 joined by dots, e.g. 192.168.1.10About 4.3 billion (232)
IPv6128 bits8 groups of 4 hex digits joined by colons, e.g. 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:00012128
MAC48 bits12 hex digits, e.g. 00-1A-2B-3C-4D-5EBurnt into the network card
  • An IP address is a logical address given by the network; it can change. A MAC address is the physical address of the network card (NIC) and is fixed by the maker.
  • IPv4 classes by first number: A 1 to 126, B 128 to 191, C 192 to 223, D 224 to 239 (multicast), E 240 to 255 (research). 127.0.0.1 is the loopback address (this computer itself).
  • Private ranges, used inside home and office networks: 10.x.x.x, 172.16.x.x to 172.31.x.x, 192.168.x.x.
  • DNS (Domain Name System) turns a domain name such as www.example.com into an IP address, like a phone book.
  • DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) gives devices an IP address automatically when they join a network.
  • NAT lets many devices with private addresses share one public IP address.

Mini example: each part of an IPv4 address is 8 bits (an octet), so it can be 0 to 255. 192.168.1.300 is not valid.

concepts.title: Protocols and port numbers
concepts.body:
A protocol is a set of rules for communication. A port number tells the receiving computer which service the data is for.

ProtocolFull formJobPort
HTTPHyperText Transfer ProtocolWeb pages80
HTTPSHTTP Secure (HTTP over SSL/TLS)Encrypted web pages443
FTPFile Transfer ProtocolUpload and download files20 (data), 21 (control)
SSHSecure ShellSecure remote login22
TelnetTeletype NetworkRemote login, not encrypted23
SMTPSimple Mail Transfer ProtocolSending email25 (587 for clients)
DNSDomain Name SystemName to IP address53
DHCPDynamic Host Configuration ProtocolGives IP addresses67, 68
POP3Post Office Protocol version 3Download email110 (995 secure)
IMAPInternet Message Access ProtocolRead email kept on the server143 (993 secure)
NTPNetwork Time ProtocolSync clocks123
SNMPSimple Network Management ProtocolManage network devices161
RDPRemote Desktop ProtocolWindows remote desktop3389
  • TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is connection-oriented and reliable: it checks that every packet arrives in order. Used by web, email and file transfer.
  • UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is connectionless and faster but does not guarantee delivery. Used by live video, online games, voice calls and DNS lookups.
  • IP (Internet Protocol) addresses and routes packets. TCP/IP together are the base of the Internet.
  • Uploading sends data from your computer to a server. Downloading brings data from a server to your computer.
  • SSL/TLS (Secure Sockets Layer / Transport Layer Security) encrypts data in transit; the padlock in the address bar shows it is in use.
  • VoIP carries voice calls over the Internet.

concepts.title: Email
concepts.body:
FieldMeaning
ToMain receiver
CC (Carbon Copy)Copy to others; every receiver can see these addresses
BCC (Blind Carbon Copy)Copy to others; these addresses are hidden from all other receivers
SubjectOne-line topic of the mail
AttachmentA file sent with the mail (shown by a paper clip)
SignatureText added automatically at the end, such as name and phone
  • An email address is username@domain, for example ravi@example.com. The first networked email was sent by Ray Tomlinson in 1971; he chose the @ sign.
  • Folders: Inbox (received), Drafts (unfinished), Sent, Outbox (waiting to be sent), Spam or Junk (unwanted bulk mail), Trash or Bin (deleted), Archive (removed from Inbox but kept).
  • Reply answers only the sender; Reply All answers the sender and everyone in To and CC; Forward sends the mail on to someone new.
  • SMTP sends mail. POP3 downloads mail to one device and usually removes it from the server. IMAP keeps mail on the server and syncs it across all devices. MIME lets mail carry attachments, pictures and non-English text.
  • Email service providers (webmail): Gmail (Google), Outlook.com (Microsoft), Yahoo Mail, Yandex Mail (Russia), Zoho Mail and Rediffmail (India), Proton Mail. Email clients (programs): Microsoft Outlook, Mozilla Thunderbird, Apple Mail.
Gmail key (keyboard shortcuts turned on)What it does
cCompose a new message
r, a, fReply, reply all, forward
eArchive
#Delete
/Search mail
j, kOlder, newer conversation
Ctrl+EnterSend

In Microsoft Outlook: Ctrl+N new mail, Ctrl+R reply, Ctrl+Shift+R reply all, Ctrl+F forward, Ctrl+Enter or Alt+S send.

concepts.title: Network types, topologies and media
concepts.body:
TypeFull formArea
PANPersonal Area NetworkAround one person, about 10 m (Bluetooth, phone to earbuds)
LANLocal Area NetworkOne room, building or campus (office Wi-Fi, Ethernet)
CANCampus Area NetworkSeveral buildings of a university or company
MANMetropolitan Area NetworkA city (cable TV network)
WANWide Area NetworkA country or the world; the Internet is the largest WAN. Uses optical fibre, leased lines and satellite links.
TopologyLayoutKey point
BusAll devices on one backbone cableCheap; one cable break stops everyone
StarAll devices to one central hub or switchEasy to add devices; if the centre fails, all stop
RingEach device joined to two neighbours in a loopData goes one way round; one break can stop the ring
MeshEvery device joined to every otherMost reliable; needs n(n − 1)/2 cables for n devices
TreeStars joined in a hierarchyEasy to expand
HybridMix of two or moreFlexible

Mini example: a full mesh of 6 computers needs 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15 cables.

  • Wired media: twisted pair (Ethernet cable with RJ-45 plug), coaxial cable (cable TV), optical fibre (light pulses; fastest, long distance, not affected by electrical noise).
  • Wireless: Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11), Bluetooth, infrared, microwave, satellite. Wired Ethernet is IEEE 802.3.
  • Transmission modes: simplex one way only (keyboard to computer, TV broadcast); half-duplex both ways but one at a time (walkie-talkie); full-duplex both ways at once (telephone call).
  • Bandwidth or bit rate is how much data can move per second, measured in bits per second (bps, kbps, Mbps, Gbps).
  • Client-server: a central server serves many clients. Peer-to-peer: every computer is equal and shares directly.

concepts.title: Network devices and connectors
concepts.body:
DeviceOSI layerWhat it does
Repeater1 PhysicalRegenerates a weak signal so it can travel further
Hub1 PhysicalSends incoming data to every port (broadcast); no intelligence
Bridge2 Data linkJoins two LAN segments and filters traffic using MAC addresses
Switch2 Data linkSends data only to the port of the target device, using its MAC address (a multiport bridge)
Router3 NetworkJoins different networks and picks the best path for packets using IP addresses
GatewayAll layersA passage between two networks that may use different protocols or models; it converts between them
Modem1 PhysicalMOdulator-DEModulator: turns digital signals into analog for phone or cable lines and back
NIC2 Data linkNetwork Interface Card; holds the MAC address
Access point2 Data linkLets Wi-Fi devices join a wired LAN
Firewall3 and aboveAllows or blocks traffic by rules
ConnectorKey fact
VGA15 pins (holes) in 3 rows; analog video to a monitor
HDMIDigital video and audio in one cable; 19 pins (standard type A)
DVIDigital (and analog) video to monitors
RJ-458 pins; Ethernet network cable
RJ-11Telephone line and dial-up modem
USBUniversal Serial Bus; data and power for many devices

concepts.title: OSI and TCP/IP models
concepts.body:
The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model from ISO splits networking into 7 layers. Bottom to top: Physical, Data link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. Memory aid: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.

LayerJobExamplesData unit
7 ApplicationServices the user sees: web, email, file transferHTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNSData
6 PresentationTranslation, encryption, compression of dataJPEG, MPEG, SSL/TLSData
5 SessionOpens, manages and closes sessions (dialog control)NetBIOS, RPCData
4 TransportEnd-to-end delivery, error control, portsTCP, UDPSegment
3 NetworkLogical (IP) addressing and routing between networksIP, ICMP; routerPacket
2 Data linkPhysical (MAC) addressing, framing, error detection on one linkEthernet; switch, bridgeFrame
1 PhysicalSends raw bits over cable or airCables, hub, repeaterBit

The TCP/IP model has 4 layers: Network access (link), Internet, Transport, Application. The OSI Application, Presentation and Session layers are merged into its Application layer.

concepts.title: Staying safe online
concepts.body:
Computer security is a separate topic; here are the Internet terms that appear in this section.

ThreatWhat it is
PhishingFake email or website that pretends to be a bank or company to steal passwords
SpamUnwanted bulk email
MalwareHarmful software: virus, worm, trojan, spyware, adware, ransomware, keylogger
Tracking cookiesThird-party cookies that follow you across sites
DoS / DDoS attackFlooding a server with traffic so real users cannot reach it
Man-in-the-middleAn attacker secretly reads or changes data between two parties
ProtectionWhat it does
FirewallHardware or software that checks incoming and outgoing traffic and blocks what breaks the rules
Encryption (HTTPS, SSL/TLS)Scrambles data during transmission so only the receiver can read it
VPNVirtual Private Network: an encrypted tunnel over the public Internet
Two-factor authenticationPassword plus a second proof such as an OTP
AntivirusFinds and removes malware
CAPTCHATest that tells humans from bots

varieties.name: The web, websites and URLs
varieties.how: Keep the Internet (the network, from ARPANET 1969) separate from the WWW (linked pages, Tim Berners-Lee 1989). Split a URL into protocol, domain and path.

example.q: In the URL https://www.example.co.in/news/today.html, what is the top-level domain?
steps: The top-level domain is the last part of the domain name.

varieties.name: Browsers, cookies and browser shortcuts
varieties.how: Know who makes each browser and which engine it uses. Browser keys follow Ctrl plus the first letter (T tab, N window, H history, D bookmark); F5 or Ctrl+R reloads.

example.q: Which keyboard shortcut reloads the current page in Google Chrome?
steps: Ctrl+T opens a new tab and Ctrl+H opens history.
F5 or Ctrl+R reloads the page.

varieties.name: IP addresses, MAC and DNS
varieties.how: Remember the sizes 32, 128, 48 bits (IPv4, IPv6, MAC). IP is logical, MAC is physical. DNS turns names into IP addresses; DHCP hands out IP addresses.

example.q: How many different IPv4 addresses are possible in theory?
steps: Each bit has 2 values, so there are 2<sup>32</sup> addresses.

varieties.name: Protocols and port numbers
varieties.how: Learn each protocol with its full form, its job and its port as one line: HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, FTP 20/21, SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, DNS 53, POP3 110, IMAP 143.

example.q: Which protocol is connectionless and is preferred for live video streaming?
steps: TCP sets up a connection and resends lost packets, which adds delay.
UDP sends without a connection and without resending, so it is faster.

varieties.name: Email fields, protocols and services
varieties.how: SMTP sends; POP3 and IMAP receive. CC is visible to all; BCC is hidden. Separate providers (Gmail, Yahoo, Yandex) from client programs (Outlook, Thunderbird).

example.q: With keyboard shortcuts turned on, which key opens a new message in Gmail?
steps: r is reply and f is forward.

varieties.name: Network types, topologies and media
varieties.how: Order the types by size: PAN, LAN, CAN, MAN, WAN. For a mesh of n devices use n(n − 1)/2 links.

example.q: How many cables are needed to join 6 computers in a full mesh topology?

varieties.name: Network devices and connectors
varieties.how: Place each device on its OSI layer: hub and repeater 1, switch and bridge 2 (MAC), router 3 (IP), gateway converts between different networks.

example.q: Which device connects two networks that may use different networking models and converts between their protocols?
steps: A router joins networks that use the same protocol (IP).
A gateway translates between different protocols or models.

varieties.name: OSI and TCP/IP layers
varieties.how: Use "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away" for layers 1 to 7. Match key words: bits physical, MAC data link, IP and routing network, TCP and ports transport, encryption presentation.

example.q: Which OSI layer routes packets across different networks using logical addressing?
steps: Logical address means the IP address.
IP addressing and routing belong to layer 3.

varieties.name: Online threats and protection
varieties.how: Decide whether the question names a threat or a protection, then match by what it does: firewall filters traffic, encryption protects data in transit, phishing steals passwords with fake messages.

example.q: Which method protects sensitive information while it is being sent over a network?
steps: A firewall blocks unwanted traffic but does not hide the data itself.
Encryption scrambles the data so only the receiver can read it.

tips: Learn every protocol as full form, job and port together, e.g. SMTP, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, sends mail, port 25.
Sizes to remember: IPv4 32 bits, IPv6 128 bits, MAC 48 bits.
A device that reads IP addresses is a router (layer 3); one that reads MAC addresses is a switch or bridge (layer 2); a hub reads nothing.
The Internet is the largest WAN. Bluetooth makes a PAN.
In browsers, F5 and Ctrl+R both reload; Ctrl+Shift+T brings back a closed tab.
Gmail and Yahoo Mail are providers; Outlook (the desktop program) and Thunderbird are clients.
traps: The Internet and the WWW are different: the web is one service on the Internet.
POP3 and IMAP receive mail; SMTP only sends it.
BCC addresses are hidden from other receivers; CC addresses are not.
A modem converts digital to analog and back; it does not route packets.
Encryption belongs to the presentation layer in the OSI model, not the transport layer.

questions.q: Who invented the World Wide Web?
questions.solution: Tim Berners-Lee created the WWW in 1989 at CERN. Vint Cerf co-designed TCP/IP and Ray Tomlinson sent the first email.
BCC = Blind Carbon Copy. Addresses in BCC are not shown to the other receivers.

questions.q: A network that covers an entire city is called a:
questions.solution: MAN = Metropolitan Area Network, covering a city. LAN covers a building, PAN a single person, WAN a country or the world.

questions.q: In which topology are all computers connected to a single central hub or switch?
questions.solution: In a star topology every node has its own cable to a central hub/switch.

questions.q: Which protocol is used to transfer web pages securely, using encryption?
questions.solution: HTTPS (HTTP Secure) encrypts web traffic using TLS/SSL and uses port 443. Plain HTTP (port 80) is not encrypted.

questions.q: Which device connects two different networks and forwards data packets using IP addresses?
questions.solution: A router joins different networks and picks the path for each packet using IP addresses. A hub just broadcasts, a repeater boosts signal, a modem converts digital/analog.

questions.q: How many bits are used in an IPv6 address?
questions.solution: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses. IPv4 uses 32 bits and a MAC address has 48 bits.

questions.q: Which protocol is used to SEND email from a client to a mail server?
questions.solution: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) sends mail. POP3 and IMAP are used to receive/read it; SNMP is for network management.

flashcards.back: Domain Name System: converts domain names to IP addresses
SMTP sends email; POP3 and IMAP receive it
Hub broadcasts to all ports; switch sends only to the target device (MAC address)
